name: hair
summary: The hair on a bare head: strands lying in one direction, dark, and not made of anything a smith made.
why: Metallic 0.0, which is the whole reason this file exists. The Dark Knight's bare head
is two islands - ninety-three triangles of face and twenty-six of hair - and the hair
was assigned plate_steel. Under the sun that is a black chrome cap: a hard white
specular streak across the crown and the ground's own orange reflected off the back of
the skull, which is exactly what it looked like. Nothing on a person is metal.
Roughness 0.62, and glossier than anything else on a body deliberately. Skin is 0.78 and
leather 0.72; hair is the one dielectric on a character that really does catch a
directional sheen, and taking it all the way down to skin's value makes the crown read
as felt. The number is a long way from a mirror all the same - the previous fault was a
reflection, not a highlight, and it came from the metallic flag rather than from this.
The grain is the strands, brushed along v. MU paints the strand shading into the sheet
already, so the depth is low: this is here to keep the sheen from lying flat across the
whole crown as one sheet of gloss, not to invent hair the art does not have. The scale
is finer than timber's and coarser than steel's - a strand is thinner than a plank and
thicker than a mill line.
Colour is the sheet's, and the sheet's is nearly black. That is MU's own art and not
something to correct here: skin_wizard_01 paints the Dark Knight's hair as a very dark
brown-black with the highlights drawn on, and the whole point of a dielectric is that it
keeps its own colour rather than tinting a reflection.

Roughness 0.62 -> 0.85, and the direction is the finding. On the bare Dark Knight the hair is flat single-sided fins of near-black texels, and at 0.62 the bench dome's brightness came back off them as a broad grazing sheen - a pale translucent wedge over the face and another down the chest, chased in Blender through cutout theories and UV theories before killing the specular proved it in one frame. A dark surface's sheen is most of what the eye reads on it, and on a fin card it swallows the silhouette. Near-matte keeps the spikes black; the brushed grain still varies the little that remains.
